This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

<output>
# Dust

A small command-line tool to quickly see which directories and files are using the most disk space.

Demo:

![Example](media/snap.png)

Overview

Dust prints a compact view of the biggest subdirectories or files. It automatically recurses into large subtrees so you can quickly find the biggest consumers of disk space. The display uses bars and colors to indicate relative usage and which parent folders subfolders belong to.

Usage

```
Usage: dust
Usage: dust <dir>
Usage: dust <dir> <another_dir> <and_more>
Usage: dust -p  (full-path - Show fullpath of the subdirectories)
Usage: dust -s  (apparent-size - shows the length of the file as opposed to the amount of disk space it uses)
Usage: dust -n 30  (Shows 30 directories instead of the default [default is terminal height])
Usage: dust -d 3  (Shows 3 levels of subdirectories)
Usage: dust -D (Show only directories)
Usage: dust -F (Show only files - finds your largest files)
Usage: dust -r (reverse order of output)
Usage: dust -o si/b/kb/kib/mb/mib/gb/gib (output format)
Usage: dust -X ignore  (ignore all files and directories with the name 'ignore')
Usage: dust -x (Only show directories on the same filesystem)
Usage: dust -b (Do not show percentages or draw ASCII bars)
Usage: dust -B (--bars-on-right - Percent bars moved to right side of screen)
Usage: dust -i (Do not show hidden files)
Usage: dust -c (No colors [monochrome])
Usage: dust -C (Force colors)
Usage: dust -f (Count files instead of diskspace)
Usage: dust -t (Group by filetype)
Usage: dust -z 10M (min-size, Only include files larger than 10M)
Usage: dust -e regex (Only include files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -v regex (Exclude files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -L (dereference-links - Treat symlinks as directories)
Usage: dust -P (Disable the progress indicator)
Usage: dust -R (For screen readers. Removes bars/symbols. Adds new column: depth level.)
Usage: dust -S (Custom Stack size)
Usage: dust --skip-total (No total row will be displayed)
Usage: dust -j (Prints JSON representation of directories)
Usage: dust --files0-from=FILE (Read NUL-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --files-from=FILE (Read newline-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --collapse=node-modules (Keep node_modules collapsed in display)
```

Config

Dust can read configuration from `~/.config/dust/config.toml` or `~/.dust.toml` to set default options.

Alternatives

- NCDU
- dutree
- dua
- pdu
- dirstat-rs

  -L, --dereference-links          dereference sym links - Treat sym links as directories and go into them
  -x, --limit-filesystem           Only count the files and directories on the same filesystem as the supplied directory
  -s, --apparent-size              Use file length instead of blocks
  -r, --reverse                    Print tree upside down (biggest highest)
  -c, --no-colors                  No colors will be printed (Useful for commands like: watch)
  -C, --force-colors               Force colors print
  -b, --no-percent-bars            No percent bars or percentages will be displayed
  -B, --bars-on-right              percent bars moved to right side of screen
  -z, --min-size <MIN_SIZE>        Minimum size file to include in output

      --skip-total                 No total row will be displayed
  -f, --filecount                  Directory 'size' is number of child files instead of disk size
  -i, --ignore-hidden              Do not display hidden files
  -v, --invert-filter <REGEX>      Exclude filepaths matching this regex. To ignore png files type: -v "\.png$"
  -e, --filter <REGEX>             Only include filepaths matching this regex. For png files type: -e "\.png$"
  -t, --file-types                 show only these file types
  -w, --terminal-width <WIDTH>     Specify width of output overriding the auto detection of terminal width
  -P, --no-progress                Disable the progress indication
      --print-errors               Print path with errors
  -D, --only-dir                   Only directories will be displayed
  -F, --only-file                  Only files will be displayed. (Finds your largest files)
  -o, --output-format <FORMAT>     Changes output display size. si will print sizes in powers of 1000. b k m g t kb mb gb tb will print the whole tree in that size [possible values: si, b, k, m, g, t, kb, mb, gb, tb]
  -S, --stack-size <STACK_SIZE>    Specify memory to use as stack size - use if you see: 'fatal runtime error: stack overflow' (default low memory=1048576, high memory=1073741824)
  -j, --output-json                Output the directory tree as json to the current directory
  -M, --mtime <MTIME>              +/-n matches files modified more/less than n days ago , and n matches files modified exactly n days ago, days are rounded down.That is +n => (−∞, curr−(n+1)), n => [curr−(n+1), curr−n), and -n => (𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑟−𝑛, +∞)
  -A, --atime <ATIME>              just like -mtime, but based on file access time
  -y, --ctime <CTIME>              just like -mtime, but based on file change time

      --files-from <FILES_FROM>    Read newline-terminated paths from FILE (use `-` for stdin)
      --collapse <COLLAPSE>        Keep these directories collapsed
  -m, --filetime <FILETIME>        Directory 'size' is max filetime of child files instead of disk size. while a/c/m for last accessed/changed/modified time [possible values: a, c, m]
  -h, --help                       Print help (see more with '--help')
  -V, --version                    Print version

rm -f /tmp/colortest.out
r "stdin_tty_stderr_tty" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1"
r "stdin_null" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 < /dev/null"

r "both_null" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 2>/dev/null </dev/null"
r "stdout_tty_check" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 > /tmp/o.txt; cat /tmp/o.txt"
r "stdout_file_stdin_null" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 > /tmp/o.txt </dev/null; cat /tmp/o.txt"
r "stdout_file_stderr_null" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 > /tmp/o.txt 2>/dev/null; cat /tmp/o.txt"
r "stdout_file_both_null" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 > /tmp/o.txt 2>/dev/null </dev/null; cat /tmp/o.txt"
r "stdout_file_stderr_pipe" "./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1 2>&1 >/tmp/o.txt </dev/null | cat; cat /tmp/o.txt"
r "stdin_pipe" "echo | ./executable -P -d 0 /tmp/t1"
r "C_both_null" "./executable -P -C -d 0 /tmp/t1 2>/dev/null </dev/null"

pub fn draw_it(
    idd: InitialDisplayData,
    no_percent_bars: bool,
    terminal_width: usize,
    root_node: &DisplayNode,
    skip_total: bool,
) {
    let num_chars_needed_on_left_most = max_size_width(root_node, &idd);
    if terminal_width <= num_chars_needed_on_left_most + 2 {
    panic!("Not enough terminal width");
    }
    let allowed_width = terminal_width - num_chars_needed_on_left_most - 2;

    let num_indent_chars = 3;
    let longest_string_length =
        find_longest_dir_name(root_node, num_indent_chars, !idd.short_paths);

    let max_bar_length = if no_percent_bars || longest_string_length + 7 >= allowed_width {
        0
    } else {
        allowed_width - longest_string_length - 7
    };

    let longest_name = find_longest_name(root_node, !idd.short_paths);

    let display_data = DisplayData {
        initial: idd,
        num_chars_needed_on_left_most,
        base_size: root_node.size,
        longest_string_length,
        allowed_width,
        ls_colors: LsColors::from_env(),
    };
    let _ = longest_name;

    if display_data.initial.is_screen_reader {
        let mut lines = Vec::new();
        screen_reader_lines(root_node, 0, &display_data, longest_name, skip_total, &mut lines);
        for l in lines {
            println!("{}", l);
        }
        return;
    }

    if skip_total {
        // The root is not drawn, but it still counts as the ancestor of
        // depth 0 for the purpose of shading the bars.
        let draw_data = DrawData {
            indent: "".to_string(),
            percent_bar: vec![max_bar_length],
            display_data: &display_data,
        };
        display_children(root_node, &draw_data, max_bar_length, 1);
    } else {
        let draw_data = DrawData {
            indent: "".to_string(),
            percent_bar: vec![],
            display_data: &display_data,
        };
        display_node(root_node, &draw_data, true, true, max_bar_length, 0);
    }
}

fn screen_reader_lines(
    node: &DisplayNode,
    depth: usize,
    dd: &DisplayData,
    longest_name: usize,
    skip_total: bool,
    lines: &mut Vec<String>,
) {
    let idd = &dd.initial;
    let line = |n: &DisplayNode, d: usize, is_biggest: bool| -> String {
        let name = get_printable_name(&n.name, !idd.short_paths);
        let pad = longest_name.saturating_sub(UnicodeWidthStr::width(name.as_str()));
        let padded_name = format!("{}{}", name, " ".repeat(pad));
        let padded_name = if idd.colors_on {
            match dd.ls_colors.style_for_path(&n.name) {
                Some(style) => style.paint(&padded_name),
                None => padded_name,
            }
        } else {
            padded_name
        };
        let size = format!("{:>w$}", size_string(n.size, idd), w = dd.num_chars_needed_on_left_most);
        let size = if idd.colors_on && is_biggest {
            format!("\x1b[31m{}\x1b[0m", size)
        } else {
            size
        };
        let pct = format!("{:.0}", dd.percent_size(n) * 100.0);
        format!("{} {} {} {:>3}%", padded_name, d, size, pct)
    };
    fn rec(
        node: &DisplayNode,
        depth: usize,
        is_biggest: bool,
        dd: &DisplayData,
        line: &dyn Fn(&DisplayNode, usize, bool) -> String,
        lines: &mut Vec<String>,
    ) {
        let children: Vec<&DisplayNode> = node
            .get_children_from_node(dd.initial.is_reversed)
            .collect();
        let n = children.len();
        if dd.initial.is_reversed {
            lines.push(line(node, depth, is_biggest));
            for (count, c) in children.iter().enumerate() {
                rec(c, depth + 1, count == 0, dd, line, lines);
            }
        } else {
            for (count, c) in children.iter().enumerate() {
                rec(c, depth + 1, count == n - 1, dd, line, lines);
            }
            lines.push(line(node, depth, is_biggest));

content.text:
The implementation is complete and committed. Summary of the work:

**Approach**: I explored the original `dust` binary extensively (CLI help/version, tree rendering, bar shading, size formatting, sorting/selection heuristics, hard‑link deduplication, filters, time filters, config files, LS_COLORS handling, progress indicator, terminal detection, error/exit‑code behaviour, panic locations) and then wrote a fresh Rust implementation (`src/*.rs`, using clap/regex/serde/toml/rayon/unicode-width/libc/chrono from the local registry).

**Key behaviours reproduced**:
- Identical `-h`/`--help`/`-V` output and clap conflict/validation errors.
- Tree drawing (`┌─┴`, `├──`, `└─┬`, `│` prefixes, reversed mode, `--skip-total`), name padding/truncation with `..`, bar fill `min(B, floor(frac·B)+1)` using f32, depth‑based shading (`░▒▓`), percent rounding, `-B` mirroring, column widths and the "Not enough terminal width"/"Terminal width not wide enough…" panics at the same `src/display.rs:142:5` / `:308:5` locations.
- Size formats (human binary/SI, b/k/m/g/t/kb/…, filecount with thousands separators, filetime ISO timestamps), the quirky `-z` min‑size parser, `-M/-A/-y` day windows (UTC midnight), `-m` max aggregation.
- Heap‑based "biggest N" selection with `(size, path)` ordering, `-d`, `-D`, `-F`, `-t` (with `(others)` grouping), `--collapse`, `-X` (raw + canonical semantics), `-e/-v/-I` filtering incl. zero‑size dir dropping, `-i`, `-x`, `-L`, inode dedup (disabled with `-s`), multi‑root `(total)`.
- LS_COLORS parsing/rendering (ANSI code order, bright→256‑colour mapping, fallback chains), red "biggest" sizes, colour auto‑detection via tty on stdout/stderr/stdin, terminal width/height (`max(h-10, 20)` lines).
- Progress indicator on stderr (100 ms ticks, `Indexing:`/`Preparing:` messages, spinner, clear sequences), config files (`--config`, `~/.dust.toml`, `~/.config/dust/config.toml`), `--files-from/--files0-from`, error messages and exit codes (including the not‑found/childless‑root rule), JSON output.

`compile.sh` builds offline with cargo and produces `./executable`; build artifacts are git‑ignored.
